newsitem.title: USA: Calif. muni utilities dealt blow with downgrades.
newsitem.headline: Calif. muni utilities dealt blow with downgrades.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp on Wednesday dealt a blow to several southern California public power utilities and power projects by cutting their credit ratings, warning they would face significant challenges in a deregulated market.

The downgrades were widely anticipated. While utility competition has emerged as a national issue, California has advanced to the forefront following the recent passage of legislation to open the state's massive electricity market.

"The rules have changed for the electric utilities, especially for the municipal utilities," said Eric Tashman, a partner at the San Francisco law firm of Brown & Wood LLP and an expert on California public power finance.

"The rating adjustments reflect the uncertainties created by the introduction of competition," Tashman said. "As the rules of the game become clearer for a competitive marketplace, undoubtedly the rating evaluation will continue."
S&P lowered the ratings on about $10 billion of debt. The actions affected the Burbank Public Service Department, Los Angeles Department of Water & Power and the city of Pasadena.
S&P said the downgrades also affect wholesale utility authorities, including the Intermountain Power Agency and two southern California public power authority projects.

The rating agency said the downgrades reflected the challenges these utilities and projects would face from increasing competition driven by deregulation, compounded by their higher-than-average system costs.
In a statement, S&P said many southern California municipal utilities have high levels of debt, incurred to finance their share of high-cost regional power supplies.

"These utilities better be responsive to strategies that make them competitive," said Brad Driver, S&P associate director. "If they are not, they may be on the losing side of the new environment and will face the difficulties of lost customers and revenues."
S&P said the "winners" in a deregulated market would be those utilities that can pare their debt and reduce operating costs to bring about the lower rates needed to compete.
S&P warned, however, that public officials that oversee public power utilities may be unwilling to permit higher rates on residential customer to generate revenues to pay down debt.
Phyllis Currie, chief financial officer for the Los Angeles Department of Water & Power, said S&P's decision was "dissappointing."
"We see S&P's downgrade as reflecting the need for us to be competitive," Currie said. "I think we have the resources and that there will be the political will to take the necessary actions."
Currie said the department does not plan to issue any new long-term debt in the near-term and, therefore, does not expect the downgrade to increase its borrowing costs.
Brian Tournier, municipal bond analyst in St. Louis with A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc., said S&P's actions were "premature."

"We're entering a period in California where there is obviously going to be a significant transition," Tournier said. "For S&P to downgrade the ratings before the utilities have had a chance to outline their plans moves a little bit ahead of the curve."
Tournier said S&P's decision would hurt the utilities when they refinance their debts because the downgrades would increase their borrowing costs.
With these downgrades, S&P's Driver said the rating agency had removed all southern California utilities out of the AA category.
